sections.h2: Where do I record a deed in Muskegon County?
sections.html:
Muskegon County deeds are recorded at the register of deeds, 1903 Marquette Avenue, Suite A102, Muskegon, MI 49442, phone 231-724-6271. The office is open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., and documents are accepted for recording from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The county describes the office as the official recorder of land documents since 1859.

It records deeds, mortgages, liens, surveys, plats, land contracts, condominium documents and financing statements. It also collects the state and county real estate transfer taxes. Staff cannot prepare your paperwork, because Michigan law bars clerks from giving legal advice or drafting documents under MCL 600.916(1). The county points owners to a title company, a real estate attorney or a blank form that meets state recording standards.

sections.h2: How can I send documents to the Muskegon County register of deeds?
sections.html:
You can walk in, mail the original or file electronically. Only originals with original signatures can be recorded, so a copy or fax will be returned.

Electronic recording runs through four vendors the county names: CSC, EPN, Indecomm and Simplifile. Some documents cannot go that way.

  • Master deeds.
  • Amendments to master deeds that change a legal description and carry large drawings.
  • Plats.
  • Property transfer affidavits, which belong with the county equalization department.

Ask your title company whether it files through one of these vendors. State law lets an electronic filing's fee be paid within one business day of receipt.

The office also offers two free fraud tools. Home Security Search lets owners check the records for their own name, and Fraud Guard sends an email when your name appears on a document being recorded in the county.

sections.h2: What do recording and related fees cost in Muskegon County?
sections.html:
The county posts one schedule, effective October 1, 2016. Recording is $30 per document regardless of page count, and $4 of it goes to the Michigan State Survey and Remonumentation fund. Warranty deeds, land contracts and deeds with a covenant of warranty also need a $5 tax certificate from the county treasurer before recording.

Muskegon County register of deeds fee schedule (county Schedule of Fees page)

If you pay by check and the deed needs a tax certificate, write two checks. One goes to the register of deeds for the recording fee plus any transfer tax. The other, for $5, goes to the Muskegon County Treasurer.

sections.h2: What should a Muskegon County seller sort out before closing?
sections.html:
Start with the tax certificate, because a warranty deed cannot be recorded without one. The treasurer's stamp shows that taxes on the parcel are paid up, so any unpaid balance has to be cleared at or before closing.

Next, line up the payoff of any mortgage. When a loan is paid off, the lender records a discharge of mortgage, and the owner does not receive a new deed. You can buy a copy of either document from the register's office or through the online record search.

  • Order a copy of your current deed so the legal description in the new deed matches it exactly.
  • Ask your assessor whether a principal residence exemption is on the parcel, and rescind it if the house stops being your home.
  • Confirm the exact names of every owner, since a missing owner means a missing signature.
  • Choose a title company or attorney to prepare the deed, because the register cannot.

sections.h2: Who pays transfer tax on a Muskegon County sale?
sections.html:
The grantor, which means the seller, pays it. The county charges $0.55 per $500 of value and the state charges $3.75 per $500, each counted in full $500 steps. A sale at the county median owner-occupied value of $198,300 rounds to 397 steps, giving a $1,488.75 state tax, a $218.35 county tax and a combined $1,707.10.

Exemption codes must be written on the face of the document. Two points matter for Muskegon sellers in distress: a sheriff's deed is always exempt from the state tax but is not always exempt from the county tax, and the state act also exempts instruments given in foreclosure or in lieu of foreclosure. A deed that merely corrects a title flaw, or conveys between spouses to create or end a tenancy by the entirety, also escapes both taxes.

sections.h2: What mistakes get a Muskegon County deed rejected?
sections.html:
The office publishes fourteen recording requirements, mostly drawn from MCL 565.201. These are the ones that trip people up.

  • Names printed beneath signatures must match the notary acknowledgment.
  • Grantee addresses must be on the deed, and the drafter's name and address must appear.
  • A deed that names a surviving owner needs a certified death certificate or proof of death recorded with it.
  • Court orders must be certified and sealed by the clerk.
  • The first printed line states the single recordable event.
  • Margins are 2.5 inches at the top of page one and 0.5 inch elsewhere, in black type of at least 10 point on white paper.

To add, remove or change a name on a deed you need a new deed, not an amendment. Recording a certified death certificate removes the deceased owner's interest from a property, but the register does not issue a new deed. A paid-off mortgage produces a recorded discharge, not a new deed.

sections.h2: What is it like to sell property in Muskegon County?
sections.html:
Muskegon County sits on Lake Michigan in West Michigan. Of its 1,460 square miles, 961 are water and 499 are land. The Muskegon River empties into Muskegon Lake, Michigan's only deep water port on Lake Michigan, and White Lake and Mona Lake add to the shoreline. Cities include Muskegon, Muskegon Heights, Roosevelt Park and Norton Shores.

The Census Bureau counted 175,824 people in 2020 and estimated 177,901 in July 2025. Owners live in 78.1% of homes, the median value is $198,300, median gross rent is $1,028 and the mean commute is 21.6 minutes. The county issued 451 building permits in 2025.

The county equalization department hosts several property tax forms sellers and buyers meet. A property transfer affidavit is due from the new owner to the city or township assessor within 45 days. The principal residence exemption covers up to 18 mills of school operating tax. Poverty and disabled veteran exemptions are filed with the local assessor. The county performs the assessing for some cities and townships, and others run their own.

faqs.q: What is the address of the Muskegon County register of deeds?
faqs.a: It is 1903 Marquette Avenue, Suite A102, Muskegon, MI 49442. The phone number is 231-724-6271, and the office is open weekdays from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., with recording hours of 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

faqs.q: Can I record a copy of my signed deed?
faqs.a: No. Only documents with original signatures can be recorded in Muskegon County. Court orders must be certified and sealed by the clerk of the court, and a death certificate must be a certified copy.

faqs.q: Why do I need two checks at the register of deeds?
faqs.a: A warranty deed needs a $5 tax certificate from the county treasurer, paid by a separate check to the Muskegon County Treasurer. The other check covers the $30 recording fee and any transfer tax.

faqs.q: How much is transfer tax on a $198,300 sale?
faqs.a: The combined tax is $1,707.10: $1,488.75 for the state and $218.35 for the county. The seller owes it, unless an exemption is stated on the face of the deed.

faqs.q: How do I take a name off a deed?
faqs.a: Prepare and notarize a new deed, then record it with the register. The office cannot draft it for you, so use a title company or real estate attorney. Recording a certified death certificate removes a deceased owner without a new deed.
